intro: Looking for a keyman insurance advisor near you usually means your business depends heavily on one or two people, and you want to protect against the financial shock of losing them. You want someone local enough to talk things through properly, who can look at your situation and quote you directly. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK insurance broker, and any quote comes straight from them as a price on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a keyman insurance advisor near me usually need
need_lead: Most enquiries come from owners and directors who have realised how exposed the business would be if a vital person were suddenly gone.
needs: You run a small business where one person brings in most of the sales or holds the key technical knowledge, and you want cover arranged around them.
A lender or investor has asked what would happen to the business if a director died or became seriously ill, and you need advice before you can answer.
You are putting a shareholder protection arrangement in place and want it to sit sensibly alongside key person cover.
You have been named as a key person yourself and want to understand what cover your fellow directors are considering for you.
You want to speak to someone near you who can explain the tax treatment of any payout before you commit to a policy.
context_heading: Checking who you are dealing with
context: Insurance brokers and intermediaries in the UK must be authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority, or be appointed representatives of an authorised firm, so you can check them on the FCA register. Many brokers also belong to the British Insurance Brokers' Association, and some hold Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute.

A broker should take time to understand your demands and needs, explain the key features and exclusions of any policy, and tell you how they are paid. If a complaint is not resolved, it can go to the Financial Ombudsman Service. A local advisor is useful for face-to-face conversations, but do check their authorisation wherever they are based.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Say which role or person in the business you are thinking of covering and why they are critical to profits.
Explain how the business would be affected financially if that person were lost, in broad terms.
Mention whether a lender, investor or fellow shareholder has raised the question of key person cover.
Say whether you also want to look at shareholder protection at the same time.
Describe the type of business and how it is structured, such as a limited company or partnership.
Give your location and how far you are willing to travel to meet an advisor in person.
questions: How would you go about valuing the key person for our business?
How is a key person policy payout likely to be taxed in our circumstances?
How would this cover fit with any shareholder protection we already have or are considering?
Which policy features and exclusions should we pay closest attention to?
How are you paid for arranging this cover, and what will that mean for us?
Are you authorised by the FCA, and can you point us to your entry on the register?

faqs.q: Do I need key person cover if the business is small?
faqs.a: That depends on how much the business relies on one or two people. If profits or essential knowledge would suffer badly without them, it is worth discussing with a broker. They can help you weigh up whether cover makes sense for your situation.

faqs.q: Can key person cover be combined with shareholder protection?
faqs.a: Yes, many businesses look at the two together because they address related risks. A broker can explain how the arrangements might work alongside each other. The right structure depends on your ownership and agreements.

faqs.q: How is a key person insurance payout taxed?
faqs.a: Tax treatment varies depending on how the policy is set up and who receives the payout. A broker can explain the general position, but you may also want to take tax advice. Do not assume a payout will be tax-free.

faqs.q: How do I check that an advisor is properly authorised?
faqs.a: Insurance brokers and intermediaries must be authorised by the FCA or be appointed representatives of an authorised firm. You can check them on the FCA register before you proceed. Many also belong to BIBA, and some hold Chartered status from the Chartered Insurance Institute.
